ambiguous.why: Encryption denies access, so ISC2 doctrine treats it as Availability; a practitioner could argue the data was altered (Integrity), and modern double-extortion ransomware also breaches Confidentiality.

ambiguous.item: Firmware replaced with a tampered build
ambiguous.why: Unauthorised modification is squarely Integrity, but a tampered/bricking firmware image is often described by its availability impact on the device.
Immutability is an integrity property; the control is counted IN because its primary purpose in a ransomware scenario is restoring access to data.
It is an administrative/process control rather than a technology safeguard, but the objective it serves is recoverability, i.e. availability.

ambiguous.item: Keeping a tamper-evident audit log of who changed each record
ambiguous.why: Audit logging is usually taught as accountability supporting non-repudiation; tamper-evidence itself is an integrity property, but among the offered buckets non-repudiation is the doctrinal fit.

ambiguous.item: A private key held in your laptop's TPM chip
ambiguous.why: A bare cryptographic key can look like knowledge, but because it is bound to hardware and non-exportable, ISC2 treats the TPM-held key as possession of the device.

ambiguous.item: Separation of duties on payment approvals
ambiguous.why: Separation of duties is a managerial/administrative principle, but it is frequently enforced inside an application, so some would classify the implemented control as technical.

ambiguous.item: A badge-operated turnstile in the lobby
ambiguous.why: Classified physical here; a badge system also has a technical access-control component, and the policy governing badge issuance is administrative.

assignment.You tell a client up front that a specia: Canon III — provide diligent and competent service to principals

ambiguous.item: You report a peer who is selling leaked ISC2 exam questions to candidates
ambiguous.alternative: Canon II — act honourably, honestly, justly, responsibly and legally
ambiguous.why: Exam-integrity breaches damage the credential and the profession (Canon IV), but reporting dishonest conduct by a fellow professional is also a Canon II duty.

ambiguous.item: A client pressures you to overstate their security posture in an audit report, and you refuse
ambiguous.alternative: Canon III — provide diligent and competent service to principals
ambiguous.why: Refusing to falsify a report is fundamentally honesty (Canon II), but it also concerns the quality and truthfulness of service rendered to a principal (Canon III).

ambiguous.item: You decline to exaggerate a threat in a sales pitch to frighten a prospect into buying
ambiguous.alternative: Canon IV — advance and protect the profession
ambiguous.why: Assigned to honesty (Canon II); FUD-based selling also reflects badly on and degrades the profession, which is Canon IV territory.

ambiguous.item: You tell a client up front that a specialised cloud engagement is beyond what you are qualified to deliver
ambiguous.alternative: Canon II — act honourably, honestly, justly, responsibly and legally
ambiguous.why: 'Render only those services for which you are fully competent' sits under Canon III, but candid disclosure of limits is equally an honesty duty.

ambiguous.item: Add a clause making the hosting provider financially responsible for data loss
ambiguous.why: Contractual shifting of financial liability is transference in ISC2 terms; some frameworks call this risk sharing, and the underlying technical risk is unchanged.

ambiguous.item: Safeguarding client information is a responsibility of every employee, at every level
ambiguous.why: It is a broad statement of management intent and scope, which is policy; its non-specific, advisory tone could be read as guidance.

ambiguous.item: To report a suspected phishing email, click Report, then forward it to the security inbox
ambiguous.why: It gives ordered steps for a task (procedure), but it is short and advisory in tone compared with a formal step-numbered procedure.
